comments.content:
GPT-3.5 is sufficient. I run it 10x per comment and sample an average score. Its a lot cheaper too. Due to larger context lengths, I included fallbacks to use larger models but in an overwhelming majority of cases, it uses GPT-3.5.
The larger context length is necessary for long conversations. Perhaps it would be wiser to batch the conversation into separate jobs and always use GPT-3.5.
I think this might need to be broken down into separate tasks. Let's see after you open your pull

## Context
Implement a mechanism to reward contributors based on their comments by evaluating:
- **Word count** as a `quantitative` metric, focusing on content formatting.
- **Relevance** to the topic as outlined in the issue specification, marked as `qualitative`.
- **Clarity** of articulation, ensuring comments are easily understandable.
Exclude:
- Comments from bots.
- Bot commands, identified by syntax like `/wallet 0x...`.
Due to architectural changes, avoid generating permits in this module. Determine an appropriate return value to pass to the kernel for subsequent handling, aiming for:
1. A final permit generation interface formatted as `Record<Username, string>`, e.g., `{ "pavlovcik": "50" }`.
2. Inclusion of reward amount metadata to transparently explain the rationale behind each reward.
## Score Calculation
The final score is a product of the three metrics: `quantitative (sum)` * `qualitative` * `clarity`. Word counts are adjusted by element type, excluding blockquotes.
## Scope
Transition from the monolithic `ubiquibot` to a kernel-plugin structure, addressing:
- Migration and reimplementation of conversation rewards logic.
- Integration of "data aggregation" for activity related to issues and pull requests.
- Reward calculations based on `quantitative`, `qualitative`, and `clarity` evaluations.
- Display of scoring metrics in a detailed manner as in the current [reward comment](https://github.com/ubiquity/work.ubq.fi/issues/26#issuecomment-1996890295).
## Requirements
- Achieve 80%+ code coverage with Jest tests.
- Ensure scoring configurability, with initial hardcoding acceptable.
- Define the kernel-plugin interface, focusing on core logic testing independently of the kernel.
- Develop a method for returning structured data conducive to HTML table formatting by another plugin for comprehensive reward displays.
## Remarks
- Main entry point of old version. https://github.com/ubiquibot/comment-incentives/blob/main/src/handlers/issue/issue-closed.ts
- You can see I tried classifying contributor types for the sake of our config. At a high level we had four contributor main types: assignee, issuer (the issue author) collaborator (somebody added to the team) and contributor (default)
- We also need to be able to configure the scoring for all of those classes, and also, the scoring of commenting on the issue or the pull request. I think my mistake the first time around was collecting each of these individually then scoring. This time around I'm collecting everything at once, and then I think it makes sense to classify and score.
I'm pretty much ready to test in production. We can set up another bot app and run two in parallel, but this kernel-plugin version will not need a funded wallet linked with it.

```suggestion
    for (const comment of data.allComments) {
```
could use better naming
won't this leave untransformed comments in the array?
why pass `comments` and `commentsBody`? You can get `commentsBody` from `comments`
why is configuration read from a file and not from github action context?
OpenAI token will be read from env even in production

```suggestion
export class IssueActivity {
```
GetActivity doesn't really make sense, maybe it'd better to name it IssueActivity

```suggestion
  if (path.length < 5) {
```
we are accessing `path[4]` so length must be at least 5
I see a lot of casts in this function, are they necessary?

I think we can remove this `Promise<>` because its awaited.
Also does `null` here indicate that the request to get issue/comments/reviews failed? If so in that case it'd be better if the whole calculation failed because we don't have full data.

`_processComment` will modify the comment instead of returning the comments which I think can be confusing. I saw this approach in this code multiple times for example Modules modify the result instead of returning a fresh result. While this is not wrong I'm not really a fan of functions modifying parameters because it can lead to bugs and it's not clear to the user of the function

It's not clear from Github but I'm guessing `configuration` is of type `any`? It'd be better to make types for the whole configuration using Typebox so you can also verify it in runtime when configuration gets loaded
why do you check if `key` is property of `obj` if `Object.entries(obj)` gives you all properties?
then you can use `??` which applies only if left side is undefined or null
